t.6.68.1: But having understood the mind of that great-souled Rāghava, he turned back from that battle and then entered the city.
t.6.68.2: Remembering the slaying of those swift and mighty rākṣasas, the hero of great splendour went forth, his eyes copper-red with anger.
t.6.68.3: Then Indrajit, the mighty descendant of Pulastya and a thorn to the gods, went forth by the western gate, surrounded by rākṣasas.
t.6.68.4: Then Indrajit, seeing the two heroic brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa ready for battle, at that moment manifested his power of illusion.
t.6.68.5: Then Indrajit placed an illusory Sītā, made of māyā, upon his chariot, and, surrounding her with a great army, resolved upon her slaying.
t.6.68.6: Having resolved to bewilder them all, that most evil-minded one, determined to kill Sītā, went out to face the monkeys.
t.6.68.7: But seeing him sallying forth from the city, the forest-dwellers sprang up, greatly enraged, rocks in hand and eager for battle.
t.6.68.8: Hanūmān, that elephant among monkeys, went before them, holding aloft a very great and formidable peak of a mountain.
t.6.68.9: He saw Sītā in Indrajit's chariot, bereft of joy, wearing a single braid, wretched, her face wasted from fasting.
t.6.68.10: That beloved of Rāghava, an excellent lady clad in a single soiled garment, unwashed, with all her limbs smeared with dust and dirt.
t.6.68.11: Gazing at her for a moment and concluding that she was indeed Maithilī, Hanumān, his face overwhelmed with tears, became deeply distressed.
t.6.68.13: Wondering what he intended to accomplish, that great monkey, together with those foremost of vānaras, rushed at Rāvaṇi.
t.6.68.12: Seeing Sītā standing in the chariot, in the grip of the son of the lord of the rākṣasas, she who was stricken with grief, joyless and pitiable, he spoke to her.
t.6.68.14: Seeing that army of Vānaras, Rāvaṇi, overwhelmed with rage, drew his sword from its sheath and seized Sītā by the head.
t.6.68.15: As they looked on, Rāvaṇi struck that woman, set upon the chariot by illusion, as she cried out, “Rāma! Rāma!”
t.6.68.16: Seeing her seized by the hair, Hanumān fell into dejection; the son of Māruta shed tears born of grief from his eyes, and in anger he spoke harsh words to the son of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.68.17: O evil-minded one, to your own destruction you have seized her by her braid of hair! Though born in the family of brahmarṣis, you have taken on the nature of a rākṣasa. Shame on you, whose conduct is sinful and whose mind is like this!
t.6.68.18: O cruel, ignoble, wicked and base one, whose valour is sinful! Such a deed befits only an ignoble wretch; you have no pity, O pitiless one!
t.6.68.19: Maithilī has been torn from her home, from her kingdom, and from the hand of Rāma; what wrong has she done to you, that you wish to kill her?
t.6.68.20: Having killed Sītā, you shall by no means live long, for by this deed deserving of death you have surely fallen into my hands.
t.6.68.21: Having given up your life here, after death you will attain those worlds that belong to the slayers of women, worlds despised even by those whom the world condemns to death.
t.6.68.22: Speaking thus, Hanumān, surrounded by monkeys bearing weapons, rushed in great fury toward the son of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.68.24: Having thrown that army of monkeys into turmoil with a thousand arrows, Indrajit replied to Hanumān, the foremost of the monkeys.
t.6.68.23: As that host of forest-dwellers of great valour came rushing on, he held it back with a host of rākṣasas of terrible speed.
t.6.68.25: She for whose sake Sugrīva, you and Rāma have come here, that Vaidehī I shall kill this very day while you look on.
t.6.68.26: Having slain this woman, I shall then kill Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and you too, O monkey, and Sugrīva, and that ignoble Vibhīṣaṇa.
t.6.68.27: As for what you say, O monkey, that women must not be slain, whatever would cause pain to one's enemies, that indeed must be done.
t.6.68.28: Having spoken thus to him, Indrajit then himself struck down the weeping illusory Sītā with a sharp-edged sword.
t.6.68.29: Cut by him along the line of the sacred thread, that unfortunate woman, broad-hipped and lovely to behold, fell to the earth.
t.6.68.31: Then Indrajit himself, having slain her with a great sword, mounted his chariot and, delighted, let out a mighty roar.
t.6.68.30: Having slain that woman, Indrajit said to Hanumān: “Look, this woman of Rāma's has been struck down by me in my anger.”
t.6.68.32: The monkeys, stationed not far away, heard the sound of him as he roared with gaping mouth, having taken refuge in that stronghold.
t.6.68.33: Having thus slain Sītā, the evil-minded Rāvaṇi became exultant at heart. Seeing him so elated, the vānaras, their faces stricken with despair, all fled away.
